articles.text: Children’s Fairyland is celebrating the magic of spring with an event especially designed for the forever young at heart. Fairyland’s Mad Tea Party is the year’s first of five Happily After Hours 21+ events held at Oakland’s legendary storybook theme park. It will take place on Friday, April 24 from 6-10 p.m. The immersive adults-only Alice in Wonderland-themed party will feature Wonderland mischief and theatrical surprises, a proper tea party, local food trucks, sweet Wonderland-inspired treats, a DJ with a black light dance floor, and surprise activations throughout the park. Guests can explore the iconic park, sip on curated cocktails, mocktails, beer, wine, and other beverages. Guests can feel free to express themselves with imaginative attire, whimsical accessories, or elaborate outfits. Costumes are highly encouraged, but not required. Mad Tea Party is centered around a proper tea party at the park’s famous Jack and Jill Hill. A live DJ atop the hill will help turn the space into a whimsical world of tea, beats, and Wonderland treats. Guests can enjoy a cup of tea, themed sweets, and party favors while cabaret performers bring Alice in Wonderland to life with meandering vignettes and circus surprises. The Red Queen makes cameos throughout the evening and other performers roam the park creating wandering theatrical mischief for all to enjoy. Fairyland is a playground for the inner child of every grownup in attendance. Guests are invited to hop aboard the Jolly Trolly for delightful evening rides, play inside the Alice in Wonderland tunnel and maze, and explore other storybook sets like the Old West Junction and many more. With 10 acres of lush gardens, attractions, water features, and whimsical structures, there is something magical to discover with every corner turned. This year’s Mad Tea Party welcomes back crowd favorite DJ heyLove who blends jazz, R&B, hip-hop, house, and global rhythms into soulful, genre-defying sets. She’ll be spinning choice cuts with a black light dance floor where guests can enjoy a unique experience in the Merry Meadow under the Oakland stars in neon colored revelry. A stanchioned top of the Dragon Slide becomes an exclusive VIP lounge for a select group of people who want to enjoy an elevated experience featuring champagne, bottle service, and gorgeous photo ops. While this year’s Gilded Chrysalis Experience is completely sold out, this tier ticketing option is new and is set to become a consistent feature of the annual event. Fairyland’s Gift Shop will be open for the event where guests can find an array of adults-only merchandise rolled out for the evening and can also purchase their own copy of Fairyland’s signature piece of magical merch: the Magic Key. The newest color “All Heroes Wear Pink” was recently released and will be available on the evening of Mad Tea Party. More information and tickets are available at Fairyland.org/ mad-tea-party/. articles.text: Piedmont’s Annual Arbor and Earth Day celebration is returning on Thursday, April 23, from 3:30 - 5:30 p.m., at and outside the Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue. For this year’s event, the city is teaming up with East Bay Children & Nature, an Emeryville-based organization dedicated to fostering stronger connections for children in nature. The annual event, which originated in 2007, celebrates the nearly 9,000 trees the Public Works Department maintains in Piedmont’s parks and public spaces – as well as the city’s commitment to environmental stewardship. The event will feature East Bay Children & Nature’s signature “create-with-nature” stations that invite creativity and curiosity through play with natural materials. There will be two 20-minute sessions of nature-themed singalongs, starting at 4:15 p.m. and 5:10 p.m. The Public Works Department will be in attendance with the equipment they use in their daily work, including the Bay Area’s first fully electric closed-circuit TV sewer inspection van. Children will be able to climb up and sit in the cab of the Public Works trucks. A raffle will be included which kids can enter to win a children’s book or toy related to Earth Day. The event will also feature plant giveaways allowing guests to take home a California native plant for their gardens. Two professional arborists will be on hand to answer questions about trees or plants. The Arbor Day celebration will include the announcement of the 2026 Piedmont Heritage Trees. Nominators of selected trees will be recognized at the event and receive a Piedmont Heritage Tree lapel pin. The Heritage Tree program, now in its eighth year, aims to raise awareness of and appreciation for Piedmont’s diverse urban forest. Heritage Trees are nominated by community members and selected by the Park Commission. A child climbs into a Public Works truck at the 2024 Earth Day celebration.
articles.title: Annual Arbor Day, Earth Day celebrations return April 23

This well-loved, bighearted gentleman of six years has earned a special place with volunteers thanks to his calm nature and sweet personality. Despite his impressive size of 110 pounds, Polar Bear walks with amazing leash manners. When he sees the leash come out, he displays his joyful spirit by celebrating with an adorable happy-feet dance and head bob. Growing confidence: Polar Bear has gradually overcome some of his shyness and his confidence is growing. He gently nudges your hand to ask for pets and politely accepts treats. Polar Bear would do well with appropriately matched dog companions or as a solo dog with dog friends. He is eligible for Oakland Animal Services “Home Begin’s Here” program where potential adopters agree to give an eligible dog a home for a week Calling All Big Dog Lovers! on a trial basis. Come meet Polar Bear at Oakland Animal Services this Thursday from 12 - 6:30 pm, or this Friday, Saturday, or Sunday between 12 and 3 pm. Despite his impressive size of 110 pounds, Polar Bear walks with amazing leash manners. When he sees the leash come out, he displays his joyful spirit by celebrating with an adorable happy-feet dance and head bob. Growing confidence: Polar Bear has gradually overcome some of his shyness and his confidence is growing. He gently nudges your hand to ask for pets and politely accepts treats. Polar Bear would do well with appropriately matched dog companions or as a solo dog with dog friends. He is eligible for Oakland Animal Services “Home Begin’s Here” program where potential adopters agree to give an eligible dog a home for a week Calling All Big Dog Lovers! on a trial basis. Come meet Polar Bear at Oakland Animal Services this Thursday from 12 - 6:30 pm, or this Friday, Saturday, or Sunday between 12 and 3 pm. Potential adopters with a child younger than 12 or a dog that weighs 25 pounds more or less than l must bring them to the shelter for the meeting. For more information about adoption or how to temporarily foster a puppy or dog, contact Piedmont resident Jessica McDevitt at jessicamcdev@ gmail.com. Annual Arbor Day, Earth Day celebrations return April 23 By Jake Lannon Piedmont’s Annual Arbor and Earth Day celebration is returning on Thursday, April 23, from 3:30 - 5:30 p.m., at and outside the Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue. For this year’s event, the city is teaming up with East Bay Children & Nature, an Emeryville-based organization dedicated to fostering stronger connections for children in nature. The annual event, which originated in 2007, celebrates the nearly 9,000 trees the Public Works Department maintains in Piedmont’s parks and public spaces – as well as the city’s commitment to environmental stewardship. The event will feature East Bay Children & Nature’s signature “create-with-nature” stations that invite creativity and curiosity through play with natural materials. There will be two 20-minute sessions of nature-themed singalongs, starting at 4:15 p.m. and 5:10 p.m. The Public Works Department will be in attendance with the equipment they use in their daily work, including the Bay Area’s first fully electric closed-circuit TV sewer inspection van. Children will be able to climb up and sit in the cab of the Public Works trucks. A raffle will be included which kids can enter to win a children’s book or toy related to Earth Day. The event will also feature plant giveaways allowing guests to take home a California native plant for their gardens. Two professional arborists will be on hand to answer questions about trees or plants. The Arbor Day celebration will include the announcement of the 2026 Piedmont Heritage Trees. Nominators of selected trees will be recognized at the event and receive a Piedmont Heritage Tree lapel pin. The Heritage Tree program, now in its eighth year, aims to raise awareness of and appreciation for Piedmont’s diverse urban forest. Heritage Trees are nominated by community members and selected by the Park Commission. articles.text: Piedmont’s Park Commission has come to a final decision to designate three trees for 2026 Heritage Tree nominations. The chosen trees are a Coast live oak in Dracena Park, the Gingko street trees on King Avenue, and a Redwood tree in lower Dracena Park. Later this year, signage will be installed near the tree locations. The Coast Live Oak (Quercus Argifolia) is located in Dracena Park in the upper section at the end of the new ADA pathway. The tree was nominated by Jack & Sharona Fischrup. The tree has a circumference of over 10 feet, measuring 24 inches from the ground. Based on those measurements, it is estimated to be 150-200 years old. “In terms of heritage, what that tree has seen is massive. It’s a very healthy and happy tree. I wanted to nominate the tree so it would catch people’s attention, so you can look up and take note,” said Park Commission member Jack Fischrup, who lives near Dracena Park. The Ginkgo trees on King Avenue, nominated by Cindy Rafton, were nominated for a second time (2020 by Tina Stott). The standout traits are the yellow leaves in the Fall that line the street of King Avenue between Lincoln and Hampton. Ginkgo trees are known as “living fossils,” having existed for over 200 million years. Its fan-shaped leaves are resistant to pests, pollution, and disease. The Redwood (Sequoia sempervirens) in Dracena Park was nominated by Richard Pryzbyla and is believed to be the largest Coastal Redwood in the park based upon its diameter. The tree stands just north of the tot swings, between the path that circles the quarry and the dog park fence. Piedmont has honored over 30 trees and plans to place signage recognizing them as Heritage Trees. The signage will be bronze plaques four inches in diameter, embedded into a large rock to be placed near the tree. Currently, four signs are expected to be installed in 2026: the Magnolia at Lexford and Hampton Triangle, the Redwood in Piedmont Park, the Dawn Redwoods in lower Dracena Park, and the Poplars at the Exedra Plaza. Photos for the Heritage Trees will be released on Earth Day, Thursday, April 24.

articles.text: Piedmont Unified School District’s (PUSD) school board will convene for a regularly scheduled meeting on Wednesday, April 15, at 7:00 p.m. in the District Office’s Board Room, 760 Magnolia Avenue. The meeting will include a recommendation to appoint Adam Saville as the next Assistant Principal of Piedmont Middle School. Saville, currently the middle school’s Tech Coordinator, has 20 years of experience in public education and has experience as a school principal. Pending board approval, Saville will form a new administrative team at the middle school next year with newly promoted principal Jamie Van Kleeck. The meeting will bring more news to the middle school, as the first presentation of the evening will focus on the proposal and approval of elective courses for PMS. The presentation will outline plans to transition Health from 7th to 8th grade, introducing a 0 period P.E. to 7th/8th graders and piloting four new elective courses: Debate, Forensics, LEAD (Leadership, Empowerment, Action, Development) and Life Lab. The scope, and goals of these new courses will be described by Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich and next year’s middle school top administrators Van Kleeck and Saville. The second presentation on the evening will give an update on the Diversity, Equity, Inclusion and Belonging (DEIB) programs in the district. Director of DEIB Jen Takazawa will present the report with Dolowich. “This presentation will demonstrate impact through practical application and community partnerships as well as share metrics and data used to monitor DEIB actions and inform future work,” the board background document states. The meeting may be attended in person at 760 Magnolia Avenue, the District Office’s Board Room. The meeting is also available remotely via Zoom. us/j/86109415149.

articles.text: The Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) is rolling out the red carpet for an evening of high-stakes philanthropy. Under the theme “A Night Licensed to Give,” this year’s Spring Fling Gala invites the community to step into the world of international intrigue—not for espionage, but to fund the critical “special projects” that keep Beach, Havens, and Wildwood elementary schools at the top of their class. “We’re looking for those with a ‘License to Give’ to help us secure the assets our students need most,” said Heather Frank, PEF Executive Director. “Whether you’re a high-roller in the auction or a silent partner from home, every contribution is a move toward a more supported educational landscape.” Working with Piedmont schools, PEF has identified three key objectives for this year’s fundraising efforts: • Field Trip Transportation In the words of Lillian Round, Fourth Grade teacher at Beach, “Field trips enhance the curriculum, making it more meaningful.” By funding dedicated transportation, we ensure our young recruits can explore beyond the classroom without logistical interference. • Structured Play Structured play is the ultimate training ground. This initiative funds structured play programs that blend guided strategy with creative freedom, helping students master the art of problem-solving and empathy on the playground. • Elementary School Counseling Spring Fling continues to fund on-site counseling services to help students navigate complex emotions. As one Havens student noted, “My counselor taught me there are two sides to every story, and it is important to hear both sides,” a vital lesson for any budding diplomat. The action begins with the online auction, which is open to everyone, from Tuesday, April 14 to Tuesday, April 22. Elementary parents are invited to support these efforts by becoming a Parent Sponsor, purchasing tickets to the Gala, or attending a Parent Theme Party. Visit PiedmontSpringFling.org for all the details.

articles.text: Our galaxy is vast and uncharted, but our knowledge of space grows more every day through the hard efforts of scientists. With the use of powerful tools, scientists can venture into unknown territory. The Roman Telescope, named after NASA’s first chief astronomer Dr. Nancy Grace Roman, will give the closest view of the heart of our galaxy than ever before. Our Home Galaxy Galaxies are made up of stars, planets, and great clouds of dust and gas, all held together by gravity. However, not every galaxy looks the same. While most galaxies are spiral or ball-shaped, some are less structured and have irregular forms. Small galaxies have several thousand stars and reach a few hundred light-years across. On the other hand, large galaxies contain trillions of stars and stretch millions of lightyears. Oftentimes large galaxies have supermassive blackholes at their centers – like our own. Our solar system, located in a small arm of the Milky Way, orbits the center of the galaxy at over 500,000 miles per hour. At the center of the Milky Way lies a supermassive blackhole surrounded by an incredible number of stars. The closer to the center of the galaxy you get, the older the stars become. As far as we know, our solar system is the only one that possesses life. However, with powerful new instruments like the Roman Space Telescope, we will have the ability to look at planets beyond those in our solar system. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope With a view expected to be over 100 times greater than the Hubble Space Telescope, the Roman Space Telescope will provide the deepest view of the center of our galaxy than ever before. The Roman Space Telescope will give scientists unprecedented insight into dark energy, exoplanets, and infrared astrophysics. Planned to launch no later than May 2027, the Roman Telescope will conduct several surveys that will revolutionize astronomy and answer long existing questions about dark matter, dark energy, and exoplanets. The final survey conducted by the telescope will study the stars and exoplanets in the area around the center of the Milky Way, known as the galactic bulge. The galactic bulge region is relatively unknown to scientists, but with a method called microlensing through the Roman Space Telescope, we can study exoplanets and planetary systems farther from Earth than ever before. The Big Picture It is still not known how common planets like Earth are, but the surveys conducted by the Roman Space Telescope will provide greater context for Earth and our solar system. The results from the surveys will help scientists distinguish commonalities in the exoplanets they discover and therefore advance their knowledge of planetary formation and habitability. It is a very exciting time in astronomy! A Galaxy Near You If you would like to explore a galaxy outside our own, Chabot Space & Science Center will be hosting a spectacular sci-fi night called A Galaxy Not So Far Away on Friday, May 1st. Guests will have the opportunity to craft their own glowing swords, get a glimpse of distant planets through our historic 8” refractor telescope known as “Leah,” and discover the mechanics of robotics alongside a familiar sassy android. Then, don’t forget to snap a pic in our Galaxy Photobooth, enjoy a themed cocktail, and discover the facts behind the fiction in your favorite intergalactic fantasy movies. Perfect for fans of all ages, this is a sci-fi inspired adventure you won’t want to miss! In more great news, Sci-Fi movie nights are back at Chabot. On Monday, May 4th, bring a friend and join us for a one-nightonly screening of Star Wars: A New Hope in our state-of-theart 70-foot Planetarium dome. Come early to enjoy light bites and themed cocktails in this fun, after-hours date night under the stars. Plus, check out our NASA Ames Visitor Center and AstroLight exhibit, open late for this event. Cameron Schneider is with Chabot Space & Science Center, 10000 Skyline Blvd. in the Oakland hills. Exploring the center of our galaxy By Cameron Schneider Our galaxy is vast and uncharted, but our knowledge of space grows more every day through the hard efforts of scientists. With the use of powerful tools, scientists can venture into unknown territory. The Roman Telescope, named after NASA’s first chief astronomer Dr. Nancy Grace Roman, will give the closest view of the heart of our galaxy than ever before. Our Home Galaxy Galaxies are made up of stars, planets, and great clouds of dust and gas, all held together by gravity. However, not every galaxy looks the same. While most galaxies are spiral or ball-shaped, some are less structured and have irregular forms. Small galaxies have several thousand stars and reach a few hundred light-years across. On the other hand, large galaxies contain trillions of stars and stretch millions of lightyears. Oftentimes large galaxies have supermassive blackholes at their centers – like our own. Our solar system, located in a small arm of the Milky Way, orbits the center of the galaxy at over 500,000 miles per hour. At the center of the Milky Way lies a supermassive blackhole surrounded by an incredible number of stars. The closer to the center of the galaxy you get, the older the stars become. As far as we know, our solar system is the only one that possesses life. However, with powerful new instruments like the Roman Space Telescope, we will have the ability to look at planets beyond those in our solar system. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope With a view expected to be over 100 times greater than the Hubble Space Telescope, the Roman Space Telescope will provide the deepest view of the center of our galaxy than ever before. The Roman Space Telescope will give scientists unprecedented insight into dark energy, exoplanets, and infrared astrophysics. Planned to launch no later than May 2027, the Roman Telescope will conduct several surveys that will revolutionize astronomy and answer long existing questions about dark matter, dark energy, and exoplanets. The final survey conducted by the telescope will study the stars and exoplanets in the area around the center of the Milky Way, known as the galactic bulge. The galactic bulge region is relatively unknown to scientists, but with a method called microlensing through the Roman Space Telescope, we can study exoplanets and planetary systems farther from Earth than ever before. The Big Picture It is still not known how common planets like Earth are, but the surveys conducted by the Roman Space Telescope will provide greater context for Earth and our solar system. The results from the surveys will help scientists distinguish commonalities in the exoplanets they discover and therefore advance their knowledge of planetary formation and habitability. It is a very exciting time in astronomy! articles.text: An eventful month of March for PHS’s College and Career Center culminated with the “Future-Ready: Planning for your Career Right After High School” evening panel on Tuesday, March 31, in the Alan Harvey Theater. Panelists Ben Allen, Marco Casalaina, Doug Ireland and Abby Scott took the stage to help students understand the evolving job landscape. Around 80 attendees were on hand to hear the insights from the panelists, as moderated by Sara Ironside, Co-President of the Piedmont Parents Network. The event was predicated upon the turmoil in the job market by AI and a desire to look forward to what careers paths will lead to success. Casalaina, the Core AI and AI Futurist for Microsoft, highlighted the value of taking risks and experimenting in any field of interest. He informed the audience that this is just the beginning of AI reshaping the job market and these students in the audience will all be part of the change. “They reiterated the value of working in teams, finding hobbies and passions outside of school, and being curious and interesting people,” said Ironside. Panelist Abby Scott provided a key perspective for the students looking towards college and thinking about majors. She is the Executive Director of MBA Career Center at UC Berkeley. Piedmonter Ben Allen, CEO of Parnassus Investments, offered his outlook from a highly influential company. “All but one panelist majored in one thing and through different experiences found their current career by pivoting. Trying jobs and learning from them will prepare you for the next job or experience,” summarized College and Career Director Stefanie Manalo-LeClair. The evening also included a question and answer period, as Piedmont Education Foundation’s Kim Hunter fielded questions from the audience. The sentiment from the evening was to not panic because jobs are not going away. Those entering the job market will need to be adaptable. articles.text: This spring break, Piedmont High School French teacher Bryan Smith and Piedmont Middle School Spanish teacher Shannon Fierro took five PHS students on a week-long exchange program to Marseille and Paris, France. Students Dimitri Secor, Danny King, Thomas Moision, Jo Palsa and Miles Lee made the journey, marking the second year of the exchange program led by Smith for PHS French students. French students and teachers visited Piedmont in March and it was now their turn to host the Piedmonters. The PHS students stayed with French families and attended school during the week. The group also took part in guided trips and visited neighborhoods in the Marseille area. One highlight of the 6,000 miles voyage was a beautiful boat ride to the Chateau d’If, an old prison on an island, much like Alcatraz. The island setting was the inspiration for Alexandre Dumas’ famous masterpiece novel, The Count of Monte Cristo. Another day trip started with a train ride to Aix en Provence for a tour of the city which was home to the artist Paul Cezanne. After visiting Marseille, the group went to Paris by train on Saturday, April 11. While there they took a boat ride on the Seine River and visited Notre Dame Cathedral and the Arc de Triomphe. After the week-long adventure, the group returned home on Sunday, April 12. articles.text: Freeing Children and Young Adults from Shame, Scales and Stigma helps parents navigate discussions of weight, body image Piedmont resident and adolescent medicine specialist Lauren Hartman’s recently published book, “Freeing Children and Young Adults from Shame, Scales and Stigma,” challenges parents to rethink how they talk to their children about weight and body image. With more than two decades of experience treating adolescents with eating disorders, Hartman draws on both research and firsthand clinical experience to help adults navigate often sensitive conversations about body image, weight and overall health. “Adolescents sometimes fall through the cracks in the healthcare system,” Hartman told the Piedmont Post. “They’re often the healthiest age group physically, but so much of what impacts them is behavioral and emotional. What they really want is to be heard.” “We’ve learned that early intervention can make a huge difference. Kids can get better,” she added. That belief in prevention is at the heart of her new book. Hartman emphasizes that eating disorders are not simply about food or weight, but are deeply intertwined with mental health and identity, especially in children. She also challenges the subtle ways “diet culture” continues to shape young people’s behavior in a world where weight-loss pills have become more widely available. “When I was growing up, diet culture was more obvious,” she said. “Now it’s much more disguised as wellness or longevity. Kids think they’re just trying to be healthy, but they’re not getting the nutrition they need.” Social media, she noted, has intensified the issue. Hospitalizations for adolescent eating disorders surged during the COVID pandemic, which she attributes to increased stress and screen time. Hartman’s book includes how triggers show up in everyday life, including in doctors’ offices. While she is careful not to place blame, she acknowledges that well-intentioned advice can sometimes do harm. Freeing Children presents a case for “weight-neutral care that respects the diversity of human bodies while promoting sustainable health.” “If [physicians] tell a young person to ‘lose weight,’ that’s not really targeting something actionable,” she said. “We need to focus on things that actually support health, like reducing stress, eating regular meals, or finding Piedmont resident and adolescent medicine specialist Lauren Hartman will speak about her new book, Freeing Children and Young Adults from Shame, Scales and Stigma, at Local Economy in Oakland on Sunday, May 3 joyful ways to move the body.” For parents, the challenge can be even more complex. Many, she says, sense when something is wrong with their children but may hesitate to speak up. “I hear from parents all the time, ‘I had a feeling, but I didn’t want to make it worse,’” Hartman said. “But early conversations, even just expressing concern, can be incredibly helpful.” She encourages families to trust their instincts and to examine the messages they model at home. From casual comments about “good” and “bad” foods to the presence of a bathroom scale, these small signals can shape how children see themselves. “We’ve inherited this legacy of body criticism,” she said. “But we have the opportunity to not pass that on.” Hartman’s new book is designed to be accessible with ready-to-use resources and strategies for repair when conversations about weight and health haven’t gone as intended. “It doesn’t have to be the same story for our kids,” she said. “We can create a different environment, one that’s more compassionate, more inclusive and actually centered on health.” Hartman will speak about her book at Local Economy in Oakland on Sunday, May 3. articles.text: On Thursday, April 9, Piedmont Garden Club hosted its Best In Show flower showcase in the community hall. The dogthemed event celebrated works of horticultural, imaginative floral designs, striking photography, and detailed canine-inspired The event was inspired by the charm and pageantry of a classic dog show. For the first half of the show, judges went around to rank the presented works in the five different divisions: Floral Design, Horticulture, Photography, Botanical Art, and Needle Art. Once the ranking was completed, attendees explored the creations by Piedmont Garden Club members. After exploring the many different categories of floral art, attendees walked over to the photography exhibit. The exhibit was a short walk away from the Community Hall, in a dark room to protect the light-sensitive dog and plant photos. The mascot for the show is Monty, the first Giant Schnauzer in history to win Best in Show at the Westminster Kennel Club Dog Show – the most prestigious prize in the dog show world. “Best in Show was a wonderful collaboration that brought together our entire membership. The creativity and thoughtful detail behind every entry are what made the show such a success. There was a palpable spirit of teamwork and whimsy throughout the planning and implementation! articles.text: The San Francisco Chronicle recently honored Piedmont High’s girls’ basketball team with three selections to this year’s AllMetro Team. Sophomore Andrea Martin earned first-team honors, while junior Taylor White and sophomore Savannah Dennig were named to the second team. Piedmont finished last season with a 22-5 overall record and won its fourth consecutive Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division title. They also have four straight CIF State tournament berths, and three straight NCS Open Division appearances. “There have been a lot of fun postseason acknowledgments. Taylor White was an honorable mention for the Chronicle’s AllMetro team. Savannah Dennig also earned an All-Metro honorable mention selection. Staff Photos Andrea Martin earned firstteam All-Metro honors by the SF Chronicle. It shows a testament to all their hard work. To get one of these awards, you have to be one of the top teams,” said coach Bryan Gardere. Martin finished the season as the League Co-Player of the Year, averaging 23.5 points per game and 10.5 rebounds per game. It is the fifth year in a row for a Piedmont player to win Player of the Year in the Western Alameda County Conference. Sophomore teammate Jenelle Solis won the 2025 honor as a freshman, Natalia Martinez won in 2024 and 2023, and Trinity Zamora won in 2022. “Drea (Andrea Martin) is arguably a top-five player in Northern California. She may have been the 19th or 20th Player of the Year in my 23 years as coach in total. It’s a reflection of the whole program, Drea couldn’t do it alone,” Gardere said. White was a game-changer for Piedmont as well, often leading the team in rebounds each game. She averaged around 12 rebounds per game in 2025/2026, and noticeably improved as a scorer. “Taylor is one of the better defenders in the area for sure, but she’s adding to her skillsets. She led the team in rebounding and loads the stat sheets. She’s almost getting a triple-double every game,” Gardere said. Dennig is often viewed as a heart-and-soul type player on the team. She gives her all on every loose ball, plays stellar defense, is a skilled passer, and will nab rebounds despite not being the tallest girl on the floor. “Savannah came to high school with a super high motor and as a hustle player with skills to still improve. She’s one of those hard workers, and you see each year she’s getting better and better. She hit a behind the back, step back 3-pointer; and I was like, ‘Where did this come from?’ She’s put in so much work to add to her game, it’s really been impressive,” Gardere said. Piedmont lost Dennig for its final stretch in the playoffs after suffering an injury. Their season was a bit marred by injuries, notably losing Solis to a lengthy injury for much of the regular season.

articles.text: A familiar face to Piedmont sports fans made an appearance recently in the San Francisco Chronicle. Former PHS head basketball coach, Chris Lavdiotis, was named the newspaper’s Coach of the Year after leading San Marin, the No. 2 seed, to the Division 5 CIF State Championship on March 13, upsetting No. 2 Sylmar 89-64. Lavdiotis was Piedmont High’s coach for 24 years until 2017 when former athletic director Vic Acuna controversially declined to renew his contract. The Piedmont community came out in support of “Coach Lav” in the months to follow, but the school still pivoted away. After one season as assistant coach at California Maritime Academy, Lavdiotis coached Lowell High in San Francisco in 2018, and then became Miramonte’s head coach from 2019 to 2024. He took over San Marin in Novato for its 2024-25 season, finishing 14-13 his first year. In 2025-26, the Mustangs missed out on a berth to the Marin County League’s playoff tournament, which Lavdiotis points out was a turning point for the team. Invoking former San Francisco Giants star Hunter Pence, coach Lav found the motivation tools to push his team into North Coast Section. “It started the day we found out we weren’t given a tie-breaker play-in game for the league playoffs... In our first postseason practice, I put on the board the words “legacy” and “focus.” I told our eight seniors, they need to decide right now what they want their legacy to be,” Lavdiotis said. “We started talking, and they said let’s start by winning the first game of NCS… We had a great practice and I said, ‘It’s up to you guys to bring this level of intensity every day.’ I stole Hunter Pence’s 2012 playoffs speech; the Giants were down 0-2 on an elimination game and Pence is yelling, ‘I want one more day with you guys.’ When we knew who we were playing, I told them, ‘All we’re guaranteed is three more days together, what are we going to do with it?’ We kept it loose, fun, and focused. That’s how we set the stage,” added Lavdiotis. San Marin started its post-season run as the No. 1 seed in the Div. 4 NCS bracket, San Marin opened with a 60-46 win over No. 16 Arroyo, and beat No. 8 Del Norte 64-43 in the quarterfinals to achieve a berth in the CIF State Tournament. They wound up losing to eventual-champion Chris Lavdiotis coaching his squad at the State Final. Former PHS basketball coach Chris Lavdiotis holds the Div. 5 CIF State trophy after San Marin won the state championship this year. He coached the Highlanders for 24 years. No. 4 Mission San Jose 49-45 in the semifinals, but they would get another shot at the Warriors later on in the D5 State tourney. San Marin won all but one game in the State playoffs by a margin of at least 10 points. As the No. 3 seed that year they beat No. 14 Trinity 69-55, dominated No. 6 Woodland 69-30, and then upset No. 2 Rancho Cotate 54-47. Then, they claimed revenge over No. 1 seed Mission San Jose in the Regional Finals, winning 56-46. They learned a lot from that NCS Semifinals loss, forcing the Warriors into critical mistakes after studying their offense. “By the time we got to Mission San Jose, we knew their tiny gym was going to be packed; it was loud and raucous. How we won that game was our preparation. I called one of my former assistants at Miramonte, Rich Forslund. Mission San Jose runs a box offense, and we had two days to work on this. Rich said, “I’ll come to practice tomorrow.” I told the team ‘I’m bringing the master in.’ I told Rich, this practice was his. articles.text: Piedmont High’s swimming team is set to make its debut at the Piedmont Pool on Friday, April 17 against Castro Valley. For the first time since 2019 – seven years ago – Piedmont High School will host its first swimming event on Friday, April 17, a league meet with Castro Valley. For Piedmont High athletes and coaches, it has been no easy feat. The swimming team has split time all across the East Bay since before the pandemic, practicing at locations including Laney College, Chabot College, Concord, Hayward, Montclair, and more. With the opening of a new Piedmont pool thus week, the school’s athletic teams will finally gain some structure after more than five years of scrambling for a pool they can call their own. “Training without a home pool for so long has caused me to accept the reality of not having a consistent place to train and adapt to whatever was available,” explained swim team junior Asher Takazawa. “Over the years we’ve practiced at pools in Montclair, Emeryville, Hayward, and sometimes even farther. It hasn’t been easy, especially relying on our parents to drive us long distances to our practices before we had our driver’s licenses.” “I’m really excited about the consistency it will bring to our training and how it will help us grow stronger as a team. There’s something special about being able to train, compete, and build team culture in your own community. It also makes the sport more accessible for younger swimmers coming up, which is huge for the future of Piedmont swimming. “More than anything, it feels like an investment in us, in our team, our routines, and the pride we have representing Piedmont,” added senior Cole Carnazzo. Most of the athletes at Piedmont High weren’t even in middle school the last time their school had a public pool. And now – finally – that will change on Friday. “It means a lot to me, not just because it’s a brand new facility, but because it finally gives us a true home pool for both my club and high school team. I’ve gotten used to practicing at different pools over the years, adapting to different conditions, schedules, and commutes.“ Having everything in one place is a game changer,” Carnazzo said. “The opening of the Piedmont Pool is something really special to me,” said Takazawa. “One of my favorite memories there is when my old coach, Rob, bought me an ice cream sandwich after I lasted the longest in dropout 50s. Moments like that are what made the pool feel like more than just a place to train. Being part of the effort to support Measure UU (the bond for the new pool) and now seeing it turn into a new pool is really meaningful. It’s cool to realize that people like us played a role in making something like this happen for our community,” Piedmont enters its new home site with a boys’ team that is pushing to be one of the school’s best of all time. Nik Costello is a member of the 200 medley, 200 freestyle, and 400 freestyle relay teams which are shaping up to challenge for the Western Alameda County Conference title and a CIF State championship berth. Costello and his teammates get to show the Piedmont community their quality on Friday in a meet that starts at 3:30 p.m. “Swimming is pretty overlooked. By Jonathan Comeaux For the first time since 2019 – seven years ago – Piedmont High School will host its first swimming event on Friday, April 17, a league meet with Castro Valley. For Piedmont High athletes and coaches, it has been no easy feat. The swimming team has split time all across the East Bay since before the pandemic, practicing at locations including Laney College, Chabot College, Concord, Hayward, Montclair, and more. With the opening of a new Piedmont pool thus week, the school’s athletic teams will finally gain some structure after more than five years of scrambling for a pool they can call their own. “Training without a home pool for so long has caused me to accept the reality of not having a consistent place to train and adapt to whatever was available,” explained swim team junior Asher Takazawa. “Over the years we’ve practiced at pools in Montclair, Emeryville, Hayward, and sometimes even farther. It hasn’t been easy, especially relying on our parents to drive us long distances to our practices before we had our driver’s licenses.” “I’m really excited about the consistency it will bring to our training and how it will help us grow stronger as a team. There’s something special about being able to train, compete, and build team culture in your own community. It also makes the sport more accessible for younger swimmers coming up, which is huge for the future of Piedmont swimming. “More than anything, it feels like an investment in us, in our team, our routines, and the pride we have representing Piedmont,” added senior Cole Carnazzo. Most of the athletes at Piedmont High weren’t even in middle school the last time their school had a public pool. And now – finally – that will change on Friday. “It means a lot to me, not just because it’s a brand new facility, but because it finally gives us a true home pool for both my club and high school team. I’ve gotten used to practicing at different pools over the years, adapting to different conditions, schedules, and commutes.“ Having everything in one place is a game changer,” Carnazzo said. “The opening of the Piedmont Pool is something really special to me,” said Takazawa. “One of my favorite memories there is when my old coach, Rob, bought me an ice cream sandwich after I lasted the longest in dropout 50s. Sibley Volcanic Regional Preserve is the perfect – and closest – place to take in the array of colorful plants in the Oakland Hills. Sibley is most known for its stone labyrinths, but the sun has allowed vegetation to grow and keep the hills green. articles.text: Visit Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery on Saturday, May 2 for a chance to step beyond the garden gates and tour Ruth Bancroft’s own private iris garden. The Iris lecture and guided tour, led by members of the Mt. Diablo Iris Society, focuses on the history of Ruth’s iris collection and how to plant, care for and divide irises with demonstrations. The Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery is famous for its extensive collection of succulents, cacti, California native plants, and other drought-tolerant plants. The garden was originally planted in 1972 by Ruth when it was her private, personal garden, but is now open six days a week for the education and enjoyment of the public. Ruth created a garden full of dynamic plant combinations using drought-tolerant plants that very few other gardeners were using at the time. But long before she became known for her succulents at the Ruth Bancroft Garden, Ruth was an avid iris collector. In 1989, her garden was selected by the Garden Conservancy to be its first preservation project, and a conservation easement was established to ensure its preservation. articles.text: Oakland Museum of California’s (OMCA) exhibition, Good Fire: Tending Native Lands, exploring cultural and historical significance of Northern California’s native communities’ use of fire, is on view now through May 31. Good Fire presents the significance of intentional fire use by local tribes whose practices predate state and federal fire management systems. Brittani Orona, co-curator of the exhibition and Assistant Professor of Native American Studies at UC Davis, said the exhibition was developed in partnership with Native fire practitioners, artists, ecologists and cultural leaders. “From the very beginning, this exhibition has been shaped in close partnership with Native collaborators, whose guidance, stories, and practices are at the heart of Good Fire,” Orona said in a press release. “By looking to their leadership, the exhibition not only honors traditions of the past, but also points to the future of land stewardship, one rooted in sovereignty, respect, and the continuance of relationships between people, fire, and place.” Museum officials said the exhibition seeks to provide context for cultural burning amid a period of increasingly intense wildfires in the region. Cultural burning, sometimes referred to as “good fire,” has historically supported biodiversity, improved habitat conditions, and maintained access to plants essential for food, medicine, basketry and ceremonial traditions. The exhibition begins with an immersive environment designed to replicate aspects of a cultural burn through sound, imagery and interpretive material. A map of California tribal territories is featured to emphasize Native sovereignty and the place-based knowledge that shapes these practices. The first gallery section, “Working with Fire,” outlines the tools, ecological functions and cultural applications of cultural burning. It includes artworks by Harry Fonseca, a recorded fire story by Rumsen Ohlone artist Linda Yamane, and regalia by Tiśina Parker. Additional displays highlight fire-adapted plants and cultural items that rely on fire-managed landscapes. A second section, “Good Fire, Interrupted,” examines the consequences of colonial fire suppression policies that restricted or criminalized cultural burning. Archival photographs, firescarred tree samples and works by artists Brian D. Tripp and Saif Azzuz address the resulting ecological decline and the emergence of large-scale wildfires linked to decades of fuel buildup. The final section, “The Future of Fire,” focuses on current efforts to restore cultural burning and expand tribal leadership in land management. Short films and artworks by Native creators, as well as baskets from Pomo artists and the California Indian Basketweavers Association, document initiatives including prairie restoration, Land Back movements and collaborative cultural burns. “This exhibition centers Native fire practitioners and culture bearers, whose knowledge is grounded in the specific ecologies of their homelands and thousands of years of experimentation,” Ryder Diaz, OMCA Curator of Natural Sciences, said in a press release. “Good Fire invites visitors to expand their view of fire in Northern California and to respect and support the sovereignty of Native peoples, who have never ceded their right to care for their lands with fire,” he added. For more information, visit https://museumca.org/.

articles.text: Opera Parallèle presents the West Coast opera debut of Doubt, with music by Douglas Cuomo and a libretto by John Patrick Shanley, May 29 through 31 at Presidio Theatre in San Francisco. Based on Shanley’s Pulitzer Prize- and Tony Award-winning play, the contemporary opera features a haunting score by Douglas J. Cuomo and centers on four characters navigating suspicion, morality, and power within a Catholic school. The staging transforms the theater into a churchlike setting, placing the orchestra onstage and immersing audiences as part of the “congregation,” blurring the boundary between spectator and participant. Doubt is directed by Brian Staufenbiel and conducted by Nicole Paiement. Performances introduce a new chamber orchestra version created by the composer and an abridged libretto by Kevin Newbury. Performances are scheduled for Friday, May 29, and Saturday, May 30 at 7:30 p.m., and Sunday, May 31 at 3 p.m. at the Presidio Theatre, located at 99 Moraga Ave. The opera runs approximately 100 minutes without intermission and is sung in English with English supertitles. Tickets start at $66 and are available through the Presidio Theatre Box Office. Patrons can purchase tickets by calling (415) 960-3949 or emailing boxoffice@ presidiotheatre.org.

articles.text: Osaka-born, Berlin-based artist Chiharu Shiota’s first solo museum exhibition in the Bay Area is now on view at the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco. Titled Two Home Countries, the exhibition spans the artist’s career across installation, sculpture, video, drawing and stage design. Shiota is best known for immersive environments constructed from densely woven strands of colored yarn, and presenting large-scale installations and other works that explore themes of identity, memory and belonging. At the center of the exhibition is Diary, a monumental installation that fills the museum’s Akiko Yamazaki and Jerry Yang Pavilion. Red threads extend across the 88-foot gallery, surrounding visitors as suspended handwritten pages from Japanese soldiers and postwar German civilians hang overhead. “Shiota is interested in what remains after a person is gone,” said Chief Curator Robert Mintz. “The installation makes history feel personal, fragmented, and profoundly present.” Other works include Two Home Countries, in which a red dress unravels into cords connecting two house-like structures, as well as sketches and videos documenting Shiota’s stage design work for KINKAKUJI (The Temple of the Golden Pavilion). “Chiharu Shiota’s work resonates because it makes emotional states visible,” Asian Art Museum Director Soyoung Lee said in a press release. “Her installations speak to the experience of living between places, histories, and identities — an experience that feels increasingly familiar to many people today.” Visit https://exhibitions.asianart.org/exhibitions/chiharu-shiota-two-home-countries/ to learn more. Installation view at Asian Art Museum of San Francisco Photo by Kevin Candland

articles.text: On Friday last, the NASA spacecraft Artemis II emerged from the backside of the moon and began its extraordinary journey back to earth, ending the mission in the capsule named Integrity. It had been a stunning achievement thus far — high risk, high gain — and in its final moments, as it traveled through the earth’s atmosphere at the breathtaking speed of 25,000 mph (30 times the speed of sound), protected by a heat shield (withstanding temps of 3,000 degrees C), its rate of decent gradually slowed until the parachutes deploy. Globally watched by millions, the astronauts had safely returned, splashing down off the coast of San Diego. Bill Nelson, former Senator, astronaut, and NASA administrator, his voice filled with pride and even awe at what NASA had accomplished, predicted that the space agency would soon return to the moon where it would construct a platform/station to be use it as a launching pad for a manned mission to the planet Mars. In that moment, while the crew emerged from the capsule, surrounded by Navy Divers, Artemis II had demonstrated that not only did NASA possess the science, it also exhibited something perhaps best defined as metaphysical: was it imagination or a “celestial epiphany.” One filled with wonder and a sense of insignificance that begged the questions how and to what end? Matt Damon stars in The Martian And it was in that moment, listening to Senator Nelson, and thinking about the word imagination, I recalled having watched the award-winning film The Martian, released in 2015, and directed by the gifted Ridley Scott. It starred Matt Damon as astronaut Mark Watney, and became a compelling story of survival. articles.text: It is not atypical to skip through Netflix, for example, in search of a movie. The platform offers a written synopsis and a very short clip/trailer of their films. And this is how I came across the extraordinary BBC/Masterpiece period series (late 1700s) titled Poldark. It opens, for mere minutes, in Virginia at the close of the Revolutionary War and introduces red coat Capt. Ross Poldark (Aidan Turner). Cut to Cornwall, England, with Captain Poldark, recovered from a severe wound, on his way home to his father, the Poldark estate, and his intended, the lovely Elizabeth Chenoweth (Heida Reed). His arrival, however, is not as he imagined. After viewing only a few episodes of Poldark, I found the narrative to be a kaleidoscope of remarkable, multidimensional characters, as well as the promise of a rich production, complex plotting, and dramatic locations (to include the massive cliffs and turbulent ocean of Cornwall). All prove to be compelling. The portrayals are superb, the writing exceptional, sustained for five seasons, while offering action, adventure, and romance. If period films interest, Poldark is a must-see, master class in story-telling, beyond the reach of two-hour movies. Poldark. A BBC/Masterpiece Theater Series – Five Seasons. Starring Aidan Turner, Eleanor Thominson, Heidi Reed. Rated PG. Released in 2016. Streaming on Netflix/Prime/Fandango/PBS/ Apple Eleanor Tomlinson and Aidan Turner in Poldark

The Martian: an inspiring space drama By Chris Honoré On Friday last, the NASA spacecraft Artemis II emerged from the backside of the moon and began its extraordinary journey back to earth, ending the mission in the capsule named Integrity. It had been a stunning achievement thus far — high risk, high gain — and in its final moments, as it traveled through the earth’s atmosphere at the breathtaking speed of 25,000 mph (30 times the speed of sound), protected by a heat shield (withstanding temps of 3,000 degrees C), its rate of decent gradually slowed until the parachutes deploy. Globally watched by millions, the astronauts had safely returned, splashing down off the coast of San Diego. Bill Nelson, former Senator, astronaut, and NASA administrator, his voice filled with pride and even awe at what NASA had accomplished, predicted that the space agency would soon return to the moon where it would construct a platform/station to be use it as a launching pad for a manned mission to the planet Mars. In that moment, while the crew emerged from the capsule, surrounded by Navy Divers, Artemis II had demonstrated that not only did NASA possess the science, it also exhibited something perhaps best defined as metaphysical: was it imagination or a “celestial epiphany.” One filled with wonder and a sense of insignificance that begged the questions how and to what end? Matt Damon stars in The Martian And it was in that moment, listening to Senator Nelson, and thinking about the word imagination, I recalled having watched the award-winning film The Martian, released in 2015, and directed by the gifted Ridley Scott. It starred Matt Damon as astronaut Mark Watney, and became a compelling story of survival. I also found it strikingly similar, yet also vastly different from the film Cast Away where a lone Everyman (Tom Hanks as FedEx administrator Chuck Nolan) struggles to adapt, mentally and physically, to his isolation on an atoll in the vast Pacific while sustaining the will to survive. The Martian is simply just so well done with an excellent cast portraying NASA’s deep bench of engineers, astrophysicists, and administrators who initially assume that Mark did not survive. When they unexpectedly discover that he is alive, the narrative takes a dramatic turn, for the NASA astronaut (a botanist) and for those who are now committed to getting him home. The story is wonderfully riveting, a rich production, with Mark, in effect, offering the voice over (sharing his daily log). And with humor and tenacity he tries to realistically assess the challenges that confront him. During the first half of the 20th Century the Key System’s Number 11 electric streetcar ran directly from Oakland Avenue through what is now the park toward Piedmont Avenue. The park’s off-leash area was permanently closed last spring after the Regional Water Quality Control Board notified the City that it needed to take steps to eliminate erosion and runoff from the hillside. The City permanently closed and revegetated the hillside to allowed the City to address the problems and avoid Key System train on the Linda Park land Map of last Wednesday’s walk steep penalties for noncompliance. Piedmont Public Works “hydroseeded” the hillside with a spray of seeds, water, and mulch. This mixture formed a protective shell over the soil, helping to stabilize the slope while new grasses and other plants took root. The park’s hillside remains closed, as the revegetation is still in early stages. Signs asked visitors to stay on the path and for people and dogs to stay off the grass as it would be easily damaged. Other signage provided information about the revegetation project and the value of oak woodlands. A $5,000 donation from the Piedmont Garden Club’s Civic Improvement Committee will support this reforestation project. Piedmont’s parks have many mature oaks, but few areas are maintained as a natural oak woodland. Linda Park’s hillside with a naturally moist, northeast-facing slope makes an ideal location for this type of landscape. The walkers made their way through the park which had beautiful California poppies along the way and exited on Linda Avenue. The group went a few steps to Lake Avenue and climbed it to Sunnyside Avenue for some early Piedmont water history. The water for this area of Oakland and Piedmont in the late 19th Century was provided by the Linda Vista Reservoir. It used to be on the Lake Avenue side of that street at Sunnyside. The reservoir was built by the Oakland Water Company in 1892 and had a capacity of 4 million gallons. It was also part of a fierce “Oakland Water War” between private companies that lasted from 1866 to 1907. In 1866, Anthony Chabot founded the Contra Costa Water Company (CCWC), the first company to successfully pipe water into Oakland. Chabot also built major reservoirs including Lake Temescal in 1869 and Lake Chabot in 1876. William J. Dingee founded the Oakland Water Company in 1893. However, the company’s water work started earlier after the CCWC refused to provide water to Dingee’s properties in the Montclair and Piedmont hills. Oakland Water became a direct competitor to Chabot’s CCWC. The competition became literal warfare. Newspapers reported both companies worked to disrupt each other’s supply, engaged in rate wars, sabotaged equipment, and publicly claimed the other’s water was “unfit for human consumption”. The war ended in 1898 when Oakland Water and CCWC merged. The new company was known as the CCWC, but Dingee was in control. However, the new CCWC lasted only until 1906. The Peoples Water Company, whose president was Frank C. Havens, was created and it took control of CCWC and other local water companies 1907. Dingee’s fortunes collapsed in about 1908. One report said he was swindled by a business partner. Following the collapse of his financial empire and subsequent bankruptcy, Dingee lived out his years in obscurity in Sacramento and died in 1941 at the age of 87. articles.text: Tucked between the rugged Pacific coastline and the bustling tech corridors of Northern California, the Santa Cruz Mountains American Viticultural Area (AVA) stands as one of the state’s most distinctive wine regions. Officially established in 1981, the Santa Cruz Mountains AVA was among the first American appellations to be defined by its mountainous terrain rather than political boundaries – a reflection of the dramatic landscape that shapes its wines. Stretching across three counties – San Mateo County, Santa Clara County, and Santa Cruz County – the AVA rises from near sea level to elevations exceeding 2,600 feet. This variation creates a tapestry of microclimates, where cool ocean fog from the Pacific meets warm inland air. The result is a long growing season that allows grapes to ripen slowly, developing complexity while retaining natural acidity. The region’s history dates back to the 19th century, when pioneering winemakers first recognized its potential. Today, a mix of historic estates and small, family-run vineyards defines the area. Wineries such as Ridge Vineyards and Mount Eden Vineyards have helped cement the Santa Cruz world-class wines, particularly Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir, and Chardonnay. Unlike the expansive valley floors of Napa or Sonoma, vineyards here are often carved into steep, forested slopes. This rugged topography limits large-scale production but rewards careful, hands-on viticulture. Many growers emphasize sustainable and organic farming practices, working in harmony with the natural environment. The wines themselves reflect this balance between power and restraint. Cabernet Sauvignons from the mountains tend to be structured and age-worthy, with notes of dark fruit, graphite, and mountain herbs. Pinot Noirs, influenced by the cooling maritime air, often display bright red fruit flavors, earthy undertones, and vibrant acidity. Chardonnays range from crisp and mineral-driven to richly textured, depending on site and winemaking style. Despite its proximity to San Francisco and San Jose, the Santa Cruz Mountains AVA remains somewhat under the radar, offering a quieter, more intimate wine country experience. Narrow, winding roads lead visitors through redwood groves and scenic vistas, with tasting rooms that prioritize authenticity over grandeur. As interest grows in terroir-driven wines and sustainable practices, the Santa Cruz Mountains continues to attract attention from wine enthusiasts and critics alike. For those willing to venture off the beaten path, this storied AVA offers a compelling glimpse into California winemaking at its most nuanced and expressive. articles.text: A different kind of dental experience in the East Bay In an era where health care often feels rushed and impersonal, one Piedmont High School alumnus has built a dental practice around a guiding principle often attributed to William J. Mayo of the Mayo Clinic: “The best interest of the patient is the only interest to be considered.” Dr. Josh Bernstein, a 1975 graduate of Piedmont High, operates a boutique dental office in nearby Oakland serving patients throughout Piedmont, Berkeley, and the greater San Francisco Bay Area. His practice is widely known for natural-looking smile makeovers using porcelain veneers and advanced cosmetic dentistry—helping patients achieve confident, healthy smiles that still look entirely like themselves. “When done right, dentistry shouldn’t look like dentistry,” says Dr. Bernstein. “It should just look like you—on your best day.” Dr. Bernstein is a Clinical Instructor in Cosmetic Dentistry, and while Cosmetic Dentistry is a cornerstone of the practice, much of Dr. Bernstein’s work centers on patients who are anxious, fearful, medically compromised, or who have avoided the dentist for years. He is also a Clinical Instructor in I.V. Sedation and the author of The Book on Painless Dentistry, and he has built a reputation for making dental care accessible— even for those who once thought it was impossible. “If someone has been afraid of the dentist for 10 or 20 years, and we can help them finally feel comfortable—that’s incredibly rewarding,” he says. The practice also provides specialized care for elderly patients, individuals with dementia, and those with developmental disabilities, working alongside an anesthesiologist group to deliver hospital-level sedation in an outpatient setting. Unlike many offices, Dr. Bernstein’s practice is out-of-network with insurance providers, allowing for a more individualized personal service and a focus on the highest quality care. At the same time, his team helps patients maximize their insurance benefits by preparing and submitting their claims. Services such as porcelain veneers, Invisalign, and comprehensive restorative dentistry are tailored to each individual, with an emphasis on subtle, natural, durable results. “We’re not creating a ‘perfect’ smile,” Dr. Bernstein explains. “We’re creating your smile—just at its best.” The office itself is intentionally small, with just two operatories and a close-knit team. That scale supports a level of personal service that Dr. Bernstein Spectacular views of Piedmont and the Oakland Hills Dr. Bernstein and his entire staff are passionate about safety. believes should be standard—but rarely is. “We have a goal that is unusual these days: to run 100% on time, every day,” he says. “And every patient gets my personal cell phone number. That level of access shouldn’t be unusual—but today, it is.” Though his practice serves patients from across the Bay Area, Dr. Bernstein’s connection to Piedmont remains strong. He recalls his high school years fondly—including a second-place finish in the Piedmont High’s Leonard J. Waxdeck Birdcalling Contest, where he shaved his head to portray the bald eagle. That same clean-shaven look also coincided with his participation in the North Coast Section swimming championships, reflecting an early blend of discipline, performance, and a willingness to stand out. Today, those same qualities continue to shape his approach to dentistry. “Technology will keep evolving,” he says. “But at the end of the day, it’s all about how you treat people—that’s what counts” For more information about Dr. Bernstein’s Oakland-based cosmetic and sedation dental practice, visit www.allnewsmiles. com. articles.text: Reader Question (Tax Edition) “The hardest thing in the world to understand is income taxes.” – Albert Einstein to his accountant Leo Mattersdorf from Time Magazine Feb 1963 Question: I am confused about closing costs. What’s the difference between non-recurring and recurring closing costs and why is the buyer for my house asking me to help cover them? Answer: The second part of your question is easier: closing costs are expensive, and most buyers are cash strapped. The first part is the important one. Non-recurring closing costs are one-time expenses tied to the transaction itself: lender fees, appraisal, title insurance, escrow fees, recording charges, and similar items. Recurring closing costs are ongoing costs that get prepaid at closing, usually things like property taxes, homeowners’ insurance, mortgage interest, and sometimes HOA dues. Those are not “buying the house” fees so much as “starting the clock” expenses. Seller-paid closing costs can help the seller by keeping the deal alive without having to drop the purchase price, which may protect the appraisal and the neighborhood comps; in a cash-tight market, a buyer who needs help with closing costs may still be fully qualified to buy, so a seller credit can be the practical difference between closing and starting over. Zoo Veterinary and Animal Care staff will continue to monitor his foot closely as he grows to ensure he uses the leg properly and it doesn’t cause any complications. “I’ve had the privilege of witnessing countless rescues. There is something so deeply moving about watching our team pour themselves so completely into a single life. Their skill, their sleepless nights, and their quiet determination motivate me. I can only hope that Crimson’s story and the work at Oakland Zoo impact all of you as it does me,” says Nik Dehejia, CEO of Oakland Zoo. The Zoo is optimistic that Crimson will have a good life regardless of his history. He has been handling his bottle feedings very well, and the team is feeding him around the clock due to his very young age and needs. Although his health appears good at this time, he is at a delicate stage, and the Zoo will monitor him closely as he grows. Crimson is currently being bottle-fed every three hours by Animal Care and Veterinary staff and will continue this routine for the next few weeks. Zoo staff have the challenging task of providing the care Crimson’s mother would have offered in the wild, while also managing routine feedings and socialization, and allowing him space to exhibit wild behaviors and act as much like a wild mountain lion as possible. In the wild, mountain lion cubs need about 12-18 months with their mother to learn essential survival skills. Because Crimson is so young, he lacks the skills necessary to be released back into the wild. After he successfully rehabilitates at Oakland Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital, the Zoo hopes to introduce Crimson to Clover, the female cub rescued earlier in March who is also receiving care at Oakland Zoo. Mountain lion kittens tend to thrive with a companion, a strategy the Zoo has successfully used with other rescues, including Briar, who has become a resident at Oakland Zoo and now lives with Silverado and Coloma at the Zoo’s California Trail mountain lion habitat. While Oakland Zoo and CDFW prefer these kittens to remain in the wild, the pairing of Clover with Crimson will help improve their overall wellbeing and secure a brighter future for both cubs. CDFW follows a thorough process before starting rescue and rehabilitation efforts for wild mountain lions. In this case, Crimson was found alone and vocalizing frequently, which is unusual for a solitary mountain lion kitten to do for long periods. The National Park Service made multiple den visits, monitored GPS collar and camera data, and continued observing the kitten. NPS biologists observed that Crimson’s mother had likely moved dens, and she was not returning to care for him. After two days, he appeared noticeably weaker, having lost 10% of his body weight, prompting NPS, in close consultation with CDFW, to retrieve and relocate him for rehabilitation. articles.text: It’s not a topic most people like to consider; our dogs are the center of our lives for many years, providing joy, companionship, and laughter. One day the time will come for you to say goodbye. Perhaps they have been diagnosed with an untreatable condition, or maybe they’re just getting older. Taking the time to learn about how to care for a dog in hospice will ensure their physical needs, as well as your emotional ones, are met. At this stage, it is important to prioritize comfort, pain management, and quality of life. Pain management is essential for dogs reaching the end of their life. Work closely with a vet to manage any pain, nausea, and stress. This may involve simple prescription medication, or the use of non-FDA approved supplements (a growing number of which have been found to support aging dogs in many ways). Be sure all family members know what medications are needed and when to avoid accidentally missing a dose. To support a dog’s mobility and comfort, consider investing in equipment such as orthopedic bedding to prevent pressure sores, particularly for dogs with limited movement. You may also need some mobility aids like rugs on slippery floors, ramps for loading into the car, or harnesses/slings to assist with walking. For dogs who tend to slip, purchase non slip pads which are stuck to the dog’s paws with gentle adhesive. Hygiene and nutrition are essential to track. For a dog losing control of bowels or bladder, check regularly for wetness or soiling to keep skin clean and dry. Offer your beloved pet enticing food or use appetite stimulants to keep them at a safe weight. And finally, ensure fresh water is always accessible. Now is your moment to spend as much time as possible with your furry friend. Focus on your own mental health and preparation for goodbye by spending quality time with your dog— talking, petting, or engaging in gentle activities they enjoy will help both of you to recall positive experiences. Zoo staff have the challenging task of providing the care Crimson’s mother would have offered in the wild, while also managing routine feedings and socialization, and allowing him space to exhibit wild behaviors and act as much like a wild mountain lion as possible. In the wild, mountain lion cubs need about 12-18 months with their mother to learn essential survival skills. Because Crimson is so young, he lacks the skills necessary to be released back into the wild. After he successfully rehabilitates at Oakland Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital, the Zoo hopes to introduce Crimson to Clover, the female cub rescued earlier in March who is also receiving care at Oakland Zoo. Mountain lion kittens tend to thrive with a companion, a strategy the Zoo has successfully used with other rescues, including Briar, who has become a resident at Oakland Zoo and now lives with Silverado and Coloma at the Zoo’s California Trail mountain lion habitat. While Oakland Zoo and CDFW prefer these kittens to remain in the wild, the pairing of Clover with Crimson will help improve their overall wellbeing and secure a brighter future for both cubs. CDFW follows a thorough process before starting rescue and rehabilitation efforts for wild mountain lions. In this case, Crimson was found alone and vocalizing frequently, which is unusual for a solitary mountain lion kitten to do for long periods. The National Park Service made multiple den visits, monitored GPS collar and camera data, and continued observing the kitten. NPS biologists observed that Crimson’s mother had likely moved dens, and she was not returning to care for him. Mountain lions rarely abandon their offspring, and it is also uncommon for a mountain lion to have only one kitten in a den. While CDFW cannot officially confirm why the mother abandoned the kitten, she may have done so because of the kitten’s abnormal hind limb, specifically the missing toes, which could have triggered an instinct in the mother to relocate her other potential kittens and conserve resources by establishing a new den site. articles.text: Piedmont Church is incredibly fortunate to have Dr. Stephen Main as our Minister of Music. We consider him a treasure. He is an extraordinarily talented and award-winning musician, conductor, composer and teacher. He leads one of the most excellent and eclectic church music program in the Bay Area. The musical offerings at our church range from Greek Orthodox chants to Shaker folk music to spiritual/gospel to jazz to contemporary pieces to traditional/classical literature. While music each Sunday is typically performed by Stephen at the 3,000-pipe organ and the 35-voice choir with soloists, there often is a small to medium group of other instrumentalists accompanying the choir. Larger ensembles perform at Easter and on Choir Sunday in June. The annual Christmas concerts, which began in 2010, feature an entire symphony orchestra and 45-voice choir. Each year, there is also an Americana Sunday program and a program featuring historical French horns with no valves. In addition to directing our Chancel Choir, Stephen also conducts a handbell choir that performs five times a year. Every week is a musical surprise.
